Lessons.Title: The Effect of Extremes
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: determine how extreme values affect mean versus median and justify which measure better summarizes a given distribution; construct and interpret data sets subject to given center constraints. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 1 Lesson 10, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/10/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher roles: Addressing HSS-ID.A.1, HSS-ID.A.2, HSS-ID.A.3; Building Towards HSS-ID.A.3.

Independent example A, a hypothetical set of ten response times in seconds: 4,5,5,6,6,7,7,8,8,9. Sum 65, mean 6.5, median (6+7)/2=6.5. Replacing only the 9 with 39 raises the sum to 95, mean to 9.5, but the fifth and sixth sorted values remain 6 and 7; median is still 6.5. The extreme creates a right tail, and the mean no longer represents the central cluster well.

Constructing displays with constraints is not a routine fixed-answer problem. Example B with ten values 0,1,2,2,2,3,3,4,5,18 has median (2+3)/2=2.5 and mean 40/10=4, greater than the median. Example C -20,1,2,4,5,5,6,7,8,10 has median 5 and sum 28, mean 2.8 below the median. Multiple legitimate constructed datasets satisfy each inequality; teacher checks both the numbers and their reasoning.

Student tasks: compare dot plots before and after replacing an extreme, find both measures of center, create at least three different data values in each student-constructed set of ten or more values meeting a specified mean/median relation, and explain why one center is more resistant. Label any data as simulated unless actually collected. An extreme can be legitimate; do not automatically delete outliers.

Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, maximum 8): correct raw-data/changed-data statistics; accurate shape/tail analysis; valid constrained example with independent mean/median checks; defensible choice of center and ethical treatment of outliers. No invented classroom response or fabricated software action counts as evidence.

Source-activity A/B review, IM Algebra 1 First Edition U01:L10: Compare two gaming populations using variable and graph; create at least 10 points with three distinct values for given mean-median relations. Keep original first-party mathematical material and graphics; source artwork identity is NOT claimed. All physical/technology/partner work remains NOT_PERFORMED unless observed.

EDULYTIKS_AUTHORED_COOLDOWN (PUBLISHER_COOLDOWN_UNVERIFIED): Explain why replacing 9 by 39 changes mean 6.5 to 9.5 while median stays 6.5; defend center under skew. KeyConcepts.Title: Resistance of the median
KeyConcepts.Definition: The median depends on order positions and often changes less than mean when one end value becomes more extreme.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Sort and compare central positions after the change.
KeyConcepts.Example: Replacing 9 by 39 raises the mean but leaves the median 6.5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mean and tails
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every value contributes to the arithmetic mean, so long tails pull it toward extremes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check distribution shape and actual numerical sum.
KeyConcepts.Example: A right extreme raises mean 6.5 to 9.5 in the ten-value example.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constructing constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: A constructed data set must satisfy the exact requested mean, median, count and distinct-value constraints.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Verify using independent arithmetic, not just a sketched shape.
KeyConcepts.Example: Ten values can have median 2.5 and mean 4 when one high value stretches the right tail.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare before and after an extreme
WorkedExamples.Question: For 4,5,5,6,6,7,7,8,8,9 replace 9 with 39.
WorkedExamples.Method: Work from the original Edulytiks dataset and independently verify the stated numerical result.
Steps: Original sum=65 and ten entries yield mean=6.5.
The middle positions 5 and 6 contain 6 and 7, median=6.5.
Replacing 9 by 39 raises sum by 30 to 95.
New mean=95/10=9.5, while the middle pair and median stay unchanged.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Mean increases from 6.5 to 9.5; median remains 6.5 seconds.
WorkedExamples.Check: The changed value is still the maximum and does not displace the middle pair.

WorkedExamples.Title: Make mean above median
WorkedExamples.Question: Analyze 0,1,2,2,2,3,3,4,5,18.
WorkedExamples.Method: Work from the original Edulytiks dataset and independently verify the stated numerical result.
Steps: There are ten ordered values and more than three distinct values.
Positions five and six are 2 and 3, giving median=2.5.
The 18 is a high extreme, creating a right tail.
WorkedExamples.Check: All ten values are listed and their sum is 40.

WorkedExamples.Title: Make median above mean
WorkedExamples.Question: Analyze -20,1,2,4,5,5,6,7,8,10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Work from the original Edulytiks dataset and independently verify the stated numerical result.
Steps: Ten ordered values include at least three distinct values.
Positions five and six are both 5, so median=5.
The -20 creates a left tail that pulls the mean downward.
WorkedExamples.Check: Mean is less than median and the stated signed sum is 28.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a high outlier always changes median
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One changed maximum often preserves all central order positions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare sorted central positions, not just the extreme.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming mean always describes a typical value
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A long tail can pull mean away from most observations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare with median and the distribution shape.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An outlier may be a genuine, important observation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Investigate quality and report it transparently rather than silently removing data.

SummaryPoints: A single large extreme can dramatically increase the mean without changing the median.
For the original ten response times, mean and median both equal 6.5; replacing 9 with 39 raises mean to 9.5.
The median is often preferred when the distribution has strong skew or outliers; report the choice with evidence.
Constrained dataset construction and interpretation are open-ended teacher-reviewed tasks.
